$comment: The tenancy-declaration finding inventory: every finding harness/tenancy_check.py can report, the severity it is reported at, and the exact command that fixes it. The set of ids here is asserted equal to FINDINGS in harness/tenancy_check.py by core's suite — in BOTH directions, because a finding the inventory does not describe is a finding nobody was told about, and an inventory entry the checker cannot reach is a promise nobody keeps. This file is NOT harness/rules.json: that inventory is the contract rules in cafaye_contract.py, and a tenancy finding in there would break the assertion that the two sets are the same set. The `remediate` strings are the reason this file exists, for MD13's reason: a check that says only "not ok" makes the reader go and look, and the reader who does not look is why it is still broken next week.

findings.claim: the mechanism is bind-parameter and the parameter that carries the account is not on the declared line.
findings.remediate: pass the account where the declaration says it is passed, or change the mechanism to the one actually enforced

findings.claim: the service declares no account boundary, so its boundary can only be discovered by reading every query by hand.
findings.remediate: write tenancy.yml; schemas/tenant-isolation.schema.json is the format and docs/tenancy.md is the worked example

findings.claim: the declaration is not a YAML document core's reader accepts.
findings.remediate: run: python3 harness/bin/tenancy-check <repo> --explain, and read the file and line it names

findings.claim: a denial arm is asserted with the wrong SHAPE — an exception where the `using` clause raises nothing, or `lives_ok` where only the row's own value proves anything — so the assertion passes for a reason other than the one it claims.
findings.remediate: match the assertion to how Postgres denies it: a `select`/`delete` cross-tenant read is a `using` clause filtering the row out, which raises NOTHING and matches zero rows, so it is asserted as an empty result and never as an exception; and the `own-account` arm must read the row's own value, because `lives_ok` passes when the write matched zero rows

findings.claim: a denied write is asserted without reading the row it was aimed at, so "matched zero rows" is indistinguishable from "found nothing to do" — which is the difference between an assertion and a coincidence.
findings.remediate: pair the denied write with a read of the victim's row, scoped to that row, and declare it: a denied `update`/`delete` is asserted as `rows_affected_zero` / `assert_unchanged`, never as an absent result, because an empty result is a lie about a row that exists

findings.claim: the negative assertion for an entry point is not on the line the declaration names, so nothing asserts that account A is refused account B.
findings.remediate: write the assertion — absent, not refused — and point negative.line at the line that carries it

findings.claim: the declaration answers cross-tenant access with a refusal, which is an enumeration oracle: a 403 tells an attacker the id exists.
findings.remediate: assert absence instead (nil, [], NotFound) and say so in negative.expects; see D33

findings.claim: an entry point is declared and the scanner can no longer find it: either the scoping was dropped or the code is gone.
findings.remediate: put the tenancy key back in the statement, or delete the entry point from the declaration

findings.claim: the service says it scopes by account and declares no way it does.
findings.remediate: declare the entry points, or set accountScoped: false if the service genuinely holds no customer data

findings.claim: this checker cannot classify every account-scoped site, so this declaration is NOT proven closed and this machine cannot settle it.
findings.remediate: read the named files by hand and confirm each one is declared; the checker's scanner reads SQL and account-key predicates only

findings.claim: the service declares no account scoping and has account-scoped code, so its honest zero is not honest.
findings.remediate: declare the entry points it has, with the negative assertions it needs; an omission is not a zero

findings.claim: a declaration names a line past the end of the file.
findings.remediate: point enforced.line and negative.line at lines that exist; a line number nobody checked is the false green written down

findings.claim: a declaration names a file that is not in this repository, so the boundary it claims to enforce is nowhere.
findings.remediate: point enforced.file and negative.file at files that exist, or restore the files it names

findings.claim: the third arm of the denial shape declares this language's spelling of NOTHING as the answer to whether an account sees its own rows, so a service that returns nothing to anybody satisfies all three cases at once.
findings.remediate: point own-account at a line that reads the row's own value (checksum, status, id); a table with no policy at all is precisely what the other two arms cannot tell apart from a correct one

findings.claim: a SECURITY DEFINER function does not pin its search path, so a caller can create an object earlier in the path and have the function resolve to it with the owner's rights.
findings.remediate: add `set search_path = ''` to the function and schema-qualify every name inside it; this is advisor lint 0011, raised from WARN to a failure because in cafaye it is a tenant-crossing primitive rather than a hardening nit

findings.claim: a table this declaration covers has policies but no `alter table … enable row level security`, so the policies are never evaluated and nothing raises.
findings.remediate: add: alter table <table> enable row level security; — and keep the force line beside it, because enabling without forcing leaves the owner reading every row

findings.claim: a table this declaration covers is not set FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and Postgres does not apply row-level security to a table's OWNER — so the role that owns the table reads every row in it.
findings.remediate: add: alter table <table> force row level security; — the bit is called FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, it is separate from `enable`, and a table that is enabled without it still lets its owner read every row

findings.claim: a policy calls the identity function bare instead of as `(select …)`, so Postgres re-evaluates it once per row rather than once per statement.
findings.remediate: wrap it — `account_id = (select app.current_account())` — which is also the only spelling rls.identity's `()` requirement admits

findings.claim: a policy clause on an account-scoped table admits every row, or a policy names no role and therefore applies to PUBLIC, or the roles the declaration names and the roles the DDL binds are not the same roles, so the table's policies read as a boundary and are not one.
findings.remediate: write `to <runtime role>` and scope the clause by the identity in rls.identity; `using (true)` is not a boundary, it is the absence of one. For the role disagreement, rls.tables[].policies[].roles must name every role the `for … to …` clause names and no others

findings.claim: a policy this declaration names is not in the DDL, so the boundary is described and not enforced.
findings.remediate: write the `create policy` the declaration names, or delete it from rls.tables[].policies and let the table be what it is

findings.claim: a policy applies to a role carrying BYPASSRLS or SUPERUSER, and such a role skips every policy on every table it can read.
findings.remediate: revoke bypassrls/superuser from the runtime role, or point the policy at a role that does not have it; the runtime role needs no superuser to read its own account's rows

findings.claim: row-level-security DDL exists in the declared sources for something this declaration does not cover, so half an adoption is in the database and nobody is accountable for it.
findings.remediate: add the table and its policies to rls.tables with forced: true, or delete the enable/force/policy lines and say databaseEnforced: false — a policy nobody declared is the state this finding is named after

findings.claim: a policy is written on a foreign table or a materialized view, neither of which row-level security can constrain, so the policy is a comment on a relation that ignores it.
findings.remediate: make it a table and let the policy constrain it, or drop the policy and scope the query that reads it — a materialized snapshot of every tenant's rows is not a boundary

findings.claim: row-level-security statements were found in a source file type this checker does not parse, so the database half of this declaration is NOT proven closed and this machine cannot settle it.
findings.remediate: read the named files and confirm each policy and force bit is declared; a Rails service's migrations are .rb files, and being named here is the difference between 'I cannot see this' and a confident zero

findings.claim: a view over a table this declaration covers is not `security_invoker`, so it reads with its OWNER's privileges and the table's policies never run for the reader.
findings.remediate: recreate the view with `with (security_invoker = on)`, which needs PostgreSQL 15 or newer; without it a view is security definer by default

findings.claim: a source path the declaration names is not in this repository, so the scan read less than was declared.
findings.remediate: point the declaration's source list at paths that exist — scope.sources or rls.sources, whichever one the finding names — or add the one that is missing

findings.claim: the declaration does not satisfy schemas/tenant-isolation.schema.json.
findings.remediate: run: python3 harness/bin/tenancy-check <repo> --explain, for the constraint and the path

findings.claim: no account-scoped statement this scanner can read carries the declared tenancy key, so it found nothing to close the enumeration against.
findings.remediate: check scope.key against the column or parameter this service really scopes by; a key nothing matches is either spelled differently or lives in a language this scanner cannot classify

findings.claim: the entry point is still account-scoped, but not on the line the declaration names.
findings.remediate: move the declaration to the line that carries the tenancy key, or put the key back where the declaration says it is

findings.claim: the scanner found account-scoped access nobody declared, so the enumeration is a summary rather than a contract.
findings.remediate: add the entry point to tenancy.yml with its mechanism, its line and its negative assertion

notEnforced.claim: The three refusal vocabularies cover the six languages — that `RAISING_TOKENS` and `LIVENESS_TOKENS` name every spelling of "it raised" and "it did not raise" a service in this fleet writes.
notEnforced.why: They do not, and closing them would mean an enum of six languages' assertion libraries in core, which `test_the_three_way_denial_shape_is_required_on_every_entry_point` refuses on purpose. So the refusals are a closed list of spellings this checker KNOWS are the wrong shape, not a closed list of correct ones: an unrecognised token passes. Measured consequence, on the conforming fixture: an `update` denial arm declared as a bare `assert_equal 0` is accepted. It counts zero rows, so it is not proof the row is intact, and this checker cannot tell that from `rows_affected_zero` without owning the vocabulary. The alternative — a rule that can only fire on English-language identifiers — is a rule that gets disabled within one release, which `docs/tenancy.md` argues at length under the honest-zero heading. What is enforced is the direction that has no good spelling: every ABSENCE token is refused on a denied write, so the lie about a row that exists is caught in every language at once.

notEnforced.claim: The declared enumeration is COMPLETE — that every way this service reaches another account's data is in tenancy.yml.
notEnforced.why: It is complete only against what `scan_file` can read: a SQL statement opening on the line the tenancy key is on, or within ATTRIBUTION_WINDOW lines above it. That is the whole scanner, and it is the honest limit of a stdlib text checker — counting routes per framework gave 96 for gateway and 0 for darkroom, and the 0 was axum's fault, not darkroom's. So anything the scanner cannot classify is named, individually, by `tenancy.enumeration-partial` and exits 0. The alternative — failing a Go service because a Python checker cannot parse `#[get("/v1/assets/{id}")]` — would get the checker disabled within one release, which is worse than an admitted gap. A checker that reads as covering everything is the failure; this one states its coverage in the warning it prints.

notEnforced.claim: The negative assertion is asserted at all — that `negative.file` exists, that `negative.line` carries `expects`, is a claim about a TEST SOURCE FILE. The test is not run.
notEnforced.why: Running darkroom's suite needs its container and its Postgres; running courier's needs a mix database. A checker that started containers to see whether an isolation test passed would be red on a laptop and green on CI depending on what was running, which is precisely the defect `gate.requirement-unproven` exists to name. So this file proves the assertion is WRITTEN — a second account fixture, an absent-shaped result, at a line a reader can open — and the running of it is the gate's business, in the service. The gap is the same one MD12 names and it is a real gap: a test that is written and never run reads exactly like a test that passes.

notEnforced.claim: `enforced.line` is the ONLY place the scoping happens.
notEnforced.why: The checker reads one line and asks whether it carries the tenancy key. A statement that scopes in a CTE, in a subquery, in a view, or in a repository method three layers down is scoped, and this checker can be pointed at the wrong one line of it — which is why `operation: call` exists and why a `call` is never counted as closure-checked. Declaring the line is a claim about where a reader should start reading, not a claim that scoping is impossible elsewhere. A service with two enforcement points declares two entry points.

notEnforced.claim: The account-scoped code is all inside `scope.sources`.
notEnforced.why: The scan reads exactly the paths the declaration names and walks past `.git`, `node_modules`, `vendor`, `target`, `deps`, `_build` and their siblings. A service that scopes in a directory it did not declare gets an honest scan of the directory it did declare, and `tenancy.scan-narrowed` fires only when a declared path is not there — not when an undeclared one exists, because this checker does not know what a service's source tree looks like. That asymmetry is deliberate: widening the scan to the whole repository is what makes a checker's answer depend on whether a dependency has been installed.

It is not, and that is the intended trade: the line is exact, so a query that moves three lines down is `tenancy.scope-lost` until the declaration moves with it, and the message says which of the two things happened. The alternative — a line number that floats within a window — cannot distinguish "the predicate is on the next line" from "the predicate is gone", and a check that cannot tell those apart reports the second one as a pass. Closure does NOT use the line: an entry point's identity is its file, its operation and its subject, so moving a query does not open ten `entry-absent` failures while dropping its predicate opens exactly one.

notEnforced.claim: The policies this declaration names are the policies the database has. Only what a `.sql` file says is read.
notEnforced.why: The row-level-security sources are read as text, so the claim is closed against the MIGRATIONS and not against the database. Three consequences, each stated rather than discovered: a Rails service's migrations are `.rb` files and a Python migration module is `.py`, so both are named by `tenancy.rls-unreadable` instead of being passed over silently — but named, not settled; a policy created in the Supabase dashboard or by an operator with a console is invisible to this checker entirely; and `REVOKE`/`GRANT` is not modelled at all, so a role that has been given table privileges is not seen. The text reading is a deliberate choice and not a limitation accepted in passing: it is the only shape that runs in a service's CI with nothing installed, and the alternative — a `pg_catalog` query like Supabase's — is a check that needs a database, which is `gate.requirement-unproven` wearing a security rule's clothes.

notEnforced.claim: A `security definer` function that reads an account-scoped table is bounded by the table's policies.
notEnforced.why: It is NOT, and this checker cannot see the function's body. What it does check is the thing that makes the body safe to reason about: with `forced: true` the function's OWNER is subject to the table's policies too, so a SECURITY DEFINER helper cannot skip them — that is exactly why `tenancy.rls-owner-bypass` is a failure and not a note. The two residual risks are real and neither is decidable from a migration file. First, a function whose owner is a superuser reads every row whatever the table says, and this checker only looks for the `BYPASSRLS` and `SUPERUSER` words on a `create role`/`alter role` line — it does not resolve a role's membership, and a role granted to a superuser role is not followed. Second, a `search_path` that is pinned but not empty is pinned to a schema the owner controls, which is a smaller version of the same hole. What is here is the checkable half; the unresolvable half is this entry.

notEnforced.claim: The declared `rls.tables` is every table in this database that carries customer rows.
notEnforced.why: It is every table the DECLARATION says, and the closure runs in one direction only: row-level-security DDL in the declared sources that the declaration does not cover is `tenancy.rls-undeclared`, a failure. The other direction cannot be closed by any stdlib text checker, because "this table holds customer rows" is a fact about the schema and a migration that says `create table uploads (id uuid, …)` with no account column and no policy looks exactly like one that does. So the honest limit is the same one the statement half already has: a table scoped in a directory `rls.sources` does not name, or carrying no account column and no policy, is not seen — and `tenancy.rls-undeclared` names the tables it DID see claiming a boundary, which is the difference between 'I found a table nobody declared' and 'no table claims a boundary'.

notEnforced.claim: A `select cafaye.protect_table('<table>')` or `select cafaye.protect_credential_table('<table>', '<digest>')` call is the boundary it writes. This checker resolves the call, not the template: the enable bit, the FORCE bit, the four `<table>_cafaye_<command>` policies and — for the credential call — the fifth `<table>_cafaye_resolve` are read from `harness/tenancy_check.py`'s own resolution of the template, not from a copy of it.
notEnforced.why: Three limits, and all three are stated in the branch that has them rather than left to be discovered. FIRST, the roles. The template writes `to %I, %I` bound to `current_user` and `coalesce(p_login_role, current_user || '_app')`, and both are decided by the session that ran the migration, so the two principals a generated policy binds are named in the template and unnameable in the text. `tenancy.rls-permissive`'s written-roles-versus-declared-roles arm is therefore skipped for a generated policy, and `rls.tables[].policies[].roles` is not compared against it — which means a declaration naming three roles where the template binds two reads green. What still runs is the half a service can get wrong: the template never leaves `to` off, so a generated policy can never apply to PUBLIC, and `tenancy.rls-role-bypass` reads the roles the DECLARATION names against the BYPASSRLS and SUPERUSER roles the migrations grant. SECOND, the table name must be a string literal, and for the credential call the digest column must be one too. A call built from a variable or a `format(...)` is not resolved, so nothing is claimed about it, the declaration's policy names resolve against nothing and `tenancy.rls-policy-absent` fires — the safe direction, since a scanner that guessed which tables a runtime-built name protects would be reporting an answer it does not have. A `protect_credential_table` with no second argument is the same refusal for the same reason and for a sharper one: the template raises `undefined_column` without it, so the call protected NOTHING, and resolving it as `protect_table` would claim four policies over a table carrying none. THIRD, the credential call's fifth policy is scoped by `cafaye.current_credential_digest()` rather than by `rls.identity`, so `tenancy.rls-permissive`'s identity arm does not apply to it — which is deliberate, because scoping a resolve policy by the account is the table-wide SELECT the mechanism exists to prevent, and it is narrower rather than missing. What still runs on it: the always-true clause arm, the per-row `(select …)` arm, the role arms, and a check that it names `cafaye.current_credential_digest()` at all, so a template that stopped writing the digest predicate is red on the one policy the exemption covers. The exemption is about the PREDICATE and not about who wrote it, so a service that wrote the five policies out by hand gets the same treatment as one that adopted the call — keying it on the call would report a false failure against the second, which is the same defect this recognition exists to end one level down. The exemption is also one arm on one policy: a credential table's other four policies still have to name `rls.identity`, so adopting the credential call does not switch the account checks off. None of the three limits can turn a red green: the enable and FORCE bits come from the template's own ordering, and a migration that calls the template has already proved at run time that the template exists, because `protect_table` raises by name if the login role is not on the cluster.
